description: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy (IEP) catalog of formal and informal logical fallacies, organized into 6 cognitive clusters.

clusters.name: Relevance & Personal Attacks
clusters.description: Arguments that distract from the core thesis by attacking the speaker or introducing irrelevant background facts.

rules.name: Ad Hominem (Abusive / Circumstantial)
rules.description: Attacking an opponent's character, background, appearance, or motives instead of engaging with their substantive argument.
detection_signals: Name-calling, insults, or impugning personal morality rather than refuting premises.
Dismissing an argument simply because the proponent stands to benefit from the conclusion.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the personal insult or motive-questioning statement and indicate what substantive argument it replaces.

rules.name: Tu Quoque (Whataboutism)
rules.description: Deflecting criticism by accusing the accuser of hypocrisy or raising unrelated counter-allegations.
detection_signals: 'What about when they did X?' or 'You do the same thing so your argument is invalid.'
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the counter-accusation and explain how it evades answering the initial point.

rules.name: Poisoning the Well
rules.description: Preemptively presenting adverse information about an opponent to discredit anything they might say beforehand.
detection_signals: Warning the audience that the opponent is an inveterate liar or corrupt before quoting them.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the preemptive disparagement aimed at invalidating future testimony.

rules.name: Genetic Fallacy
rules.description: Judging the validity of an idea purely on the basis of its origin or source history rather than its merits.
detection_signals: Rejecting an empirical claim solely because of the political or geographical origin of the speaker.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote where the origin of the argument is used as sole justification for dismissal.

clusters.name: Presumption & Circularity
clusters.description: Arguments where the premise assumes the conclusion or forces an artificially constricted set of choices.

rules.name: Begging the Question (Petitio Principii)
rules.description: An argument whose premises assume the truth of the conclusion they are supposed to prove.
detection_signals: Circular reasoning where statement A is true because of B, and B is true because of A.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the circular argument and highlight where the premise restates the conclusion.

rules.name: False Dilemma / False Dichotomy
rules.description: Presenting complex, nuanced situations as an 'either/or' choice while ignoring viable middle grounds.
detection_signals: 'You are either with us or against us' framing.
Ignoring third alternatives and treating two extremes as exhaustive.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the binary constraint and identify reasonable excluded options.

rules.name: Loaded Question
rules.description: Asking a question containing an unproven, incriminating presumption that cannot be answered simply without admitting guilt.
detection_signals: 'Have you stopped taking bribes yet?' style interrogations.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the question and identify the presupposed unproven claim.

rules.name: Cherry-Picking (Texas Sharpshooter)
rules.description: Highlighting only confirming evidence or favorable outliers while ignoring vast contradictory data.
detection_signals: Selecting isolated quarters or single studies while concealing consensus meta-analyses.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the cherry-picked dataset and identify the omitted broader body of evidence.

clusters.name: Causal & Inductive Errors
clusters.description: Inferring causation from weak correlation, sequence, or insufficient sample sizes.

rules.name: Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc
rules.description: Assuming that because Event B occurred after Event A, Event A must have caused Event B.
detection_signals: Claiming sequential coincidence proves causal linkage without mechanistic proof.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the passage asserting causation based solely on chronological order.

rules.name: Correlation as Causation
rules.description: Treating statistical correlation between two variables as definitive proof that one causes the other.
detection_signals: Overlooking confounding variables or reverse causality in statistical relationships.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the causal conclusion drawn from purely correlational data.

rules.name: Hasty Generalization
rules.description: Drawing a broad conclusion from a sample that is too small or unrepresentative.
detection_signals: Using a single personal anecdote to generalize about an entire demographic or scientific field.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the generalization and identify why the sample size is inadequate.

rules.name: Slippery Slope
rules.description: Claiming that a minor initial step will inevitably trigger a disastrous chain reaction without proving each link.
detection_signals: 'If we allow X, then catastrophic Y and apocalypse Z will unavoidable follow.'
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the predicted catastrophic progression and note the missing intermediate proofs.

clusters.name: Emotional & Manipulative Appeals
clusters.description: Substituting emotional provocation or authority pressure for reasoned argumentation.

rules.name: Appeal to Fear (Argumentum Ad Baculum / In Terrorem)
rules.description: Using fabricated, exaggerated, or apocalyptic terror scenarios to coerce acceptance of a claim.
detection_signals: Alarmist rhetoric designed to induce panic rather than explain empirical risks.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the fear-inducing rhetoric and specify how it substitutes for logical argument.

rules.name: Appeal to Outrage / Anger
rules.description: Stoking moral outrage, hostility, and indignation to bypass critical evaluation of claims.
detection_signals: Hyper-charged emotional language framing opponents as monsters or existential threats.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the inflammatory rhetoric intended to provoke outrage.

rules.name: Bandwagon / Appeal to Popularity (Ad Populum)
rules.description: Arguing that a claim must be true or good simply because many people believe or do it.
detection_signals: 'Everyone knows that X' or 'Millions of people can't be wrong.'
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the appeal to consensus or popular belief as proof of validity.

rules.name: Appeal to False Authority (Ad Verecundiam)
rules.description: Citing the opinion of a celebrity, non-expert, or authority in an unrelated field as definitive proof.
detection_signals: Using an entertainer's opinion to validate a complex epidemiological or cosmological claim.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the authority citation and specify why their expertise does not apply.

clusters.name: Ambiguity & Equivocation
clusters.description: Exploiting unclear language, shifting word meanings, or misrepresenting opposing arguments.

rules.name: Straw Man
rules.description: Misrepresenting, exaggerating, or oversimplifying an opponent's argument to make it easier to attack.
detection_signals: Distorting an opponent's moderate position into an absurd, easily dismantled caricature.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the distorted summary alongside the authentic position being caricatured.

rules.name: Equivocation
rules.description: Using a word or phrase with multiple meanings ambiguously in different parts of the argument.
detection_signals: Shifting definition of a key term mid-argument to manufacture a false conclusion.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the text and show how the key term's definition was shifted.

rules.name: Fallacy of Accent / Out of Context
rules.description: Altering the meaning of an original statement by changing vocal emphasis or removing surrounding qualifiers.
detection_signals: Selective excerpting that conveys the opposite of what the original author intended.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the excerpt and provide the missing surrounding sentences.

clusters.name: Formal & Deductive Errors
clusters.description: Structural invalidity in syllogisms and deductive logic.

rules.name: False Equivalence
rules.description: Equating two completely unequal situations, severity levels, or ethical transgressions as if they were identical.
detection_signals: Treating a minor clerical error and widespread systemic fraud as equivalent misconduct.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the comparison and explain why the two situations are fundamentally unequal.

rules.name: Affirming the Consequent
rules.description: Inferring the antecedent from the consequent (If P then Q; Q; therefore P).
detection_signals: Assuming an outcome could only have been caused by one specific prior event.
rules.evidence_guidelines: Quote the deductive statement and point out alternative possible causes.
